questions.title: How does the “absmean” quantization function compute the scaling factor γ?
questions.question_body: In the BitNet b1.58 paper the authors define the quantization function for weights as \( \widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma+\epsilon), -1, 1) \) with \( \gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}| \). I am unsure whether \(\gamma\) is recomputed for every weight matrix at every training step, or if it is a fixed statistic computed once from the initial weights. Also, what is the role of the small constant \(\epsilon\) – is it just to avoid division by zero, or does it affect the quantization granularity? Any clarification on the implementation details would help.

questions.title: Why does BitNet b1.58 use 8‑bit activations while keeping weights ternary?
questions.question_body: The paper states that BitNet b1.58 is trained with 1.58‑bit weights (\{-1,0,1\}) and 8‑bit activations. I would have expected both weights and activations to be binarized (or ternarized) to maximize efficiency. What is the motivation for keeping 8‑bit activations? Does this choice stem from accuracy considerations, hardware constraints, or the need to preserve certain non‑linear properties?

questions.title: What is the effect of removing all bias terms in the BitNet b1.58 architecture?
questions.question_body: The authors mention that they “remove all biases” to align with LLaMA‑like components. In a standard Transformer, biases are present in linear projections and feed‑forward layers. How does eliminating these biases impact the model’s expressive capacity, training dynamics, and the quantization process? Are there any empirical results comparing bias‑less vs. bias‑ful versions of BitNet?

questions.title: How is the “zero‑point” quantization avoided for activations in BitNet b1.58?
questions.question_body: The activation quantization is described as scaling to the range \([-Q_b, Q_b]\) per token instead of the usual \([0, Q_b]\) with a zero‑point. I am confused about how this per‑token scaling works in practice: is a separate scale computed for each token in the batch, and does it introduce any additional overhead? Also, how does this choice affect the distribution of activation values after the ReLU‑like non‑linearity?

questions.title: Can the 2‑bit kernel from Ladder be directly applied to ternary weights?
questions.question_body: The experimental section says that inference uses the “2‑bit kernel from Ladder” for BitNet b1.58. Since the weights are ternary (‑1, 0, +1), they technically need only 2 bits to store, but the kernel was originally designed for 2‑bit (i.e., 4‑level) quantization. How does the kernel handle the missing value (e.g., treating 0 as one of the 4 levels) and does this cause any loss of efficiency or accuracy compared to a kernel specifically optimized for ternary weights?

questions.title: What is the theoretical justification for the claimed 1.58‑bit scaling law?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that BitNet b1.58 defines a new scaling law relating model size, performance, and inference cost, and give examples such as "13B BitNet b1.58 is more efficient than 3B FP16 LLM". Is there an explicit formula or empirical fit that describes this law? How does the 1.58‑bit measure (i.e., average bits per weight) enter the scaling relationship, and does it hold across all model sizes and token budgets?

questions.title: How is energy consumption estimated for INT8 addition vs. FP16 multiplication?
questions.question_body: Figure 5 (energy) cites an energy model from prior work and claims a 71.4× reduction for matrix multiplication on 7 nm chips. I would like to understand the assumptions behind this estimate: what are the per‑operation energy costs for INT8 addition and FP16 multiplication used, and how are memory‑access costs accounted for? Also, does the energy model include the cost of converting ternary weights to the integer format used by the hardware?

questions.title: Why does the embedding layer remain full‑precision in BitNet b1.58?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that the embedding layer is not quantized, which means its memory proportion becomes smaller for larger models. Why was the embedding kept at FP16/FP32 instead of being ternarized or quantized to 8‑bit? Would quantizing the embedding break the “feature filtering” benefit of the zero weight, or is it simply a practical limitation?

questions.title: How does BitNet b1.58 achieve “feature filtering” with the zero weight value?
questions.question_body:
The authors claim that adding the zero value to the weight set (
{-1, 0, +1}) enables explicit feature filtering and improves performance over the original 1‑bit BitNet. Could someone explain the intuition behind this: how does the presence of zero weights affect the attention or feed‑forward computations, and is there any quantitative analysis showing that sparsity of zero weights correlates with better downstream performance?

questions.title: What are the challenges of extending BitNet b1.58 to Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) architectures?
questions.question_body: In the discussion, the authors mention that 1.58‑bit LLMs could alleviate the memory and communication overhead of MoE models. However, MoE typically involves routing matrices and expert-specific parameters. How would ternary quantization interact with the routing softmax and the per‑expert weight matrices? Are there any known techniques for quantizing the routing logits without degrading the expert selection quality?

questions.title: Is it possible to train BitNet b1.58 with fewer than 100 B tokens and still match FP16 performance?
questions.question_body: All experiments use 100 B tokens (or 2 T tokens for the large‑scale test). I wonder if the quantization introduces a higher data requirement for convergence. Has anyone tried training a 3 B BitNet b1.58 on, say, 30 B tokens, and if so, how does the perplexity compare to the FP16 baseline? Understanding the token‑efficiency would help assess the practicality of the approach.
